title: What a Shorter Contest Really Costs: Serial Dependence, Effective Trials, and Evidence from a Rule Change in Professional Esports

paper.title:
What a Shorter Contest Really Costs:
Serial Dependence, Effective Trials, and Evidence from a Rule Change in
Professional Esports
paper.abstract:
Abstract Operational research evaluates tournament formats by their efficacy, the
probability that the design identifies the stronger competitor, and computes it
almost exclusively by simulation under an assumption that is rarely tested: that
the trials a format aggregates are independent. We show that this assumption
systematically overstates what shortening a contest costs, and we measure the
correction. When trials are serially correlated, a format carries N / [ 1 + ( N − 1 ) ​ ρ ] N/[1+(N-1)\rho] effective trials rather than N N , so a twenty per cent cut costs
10.6 per cent of discriminating power under independence but only 5.2 per cent at
the correlation we estimate, and only 2.1 per cent in a sixty-trial format. The
ingredients are estimated from an implemented change in contest length: in
September 2023 professional Counter-Strike cut regulation rounds per map from
thirty to twenty-four. Across 72,576 maps we measure discrimination as the ability
slope over the residual standard deviation on the first half of a map, a contest
fixed by rule at fifteen or twelve rounds with no stopping rule. Against the
calibrated benchmark of 0.948, discrimination falls by thirty-five per cent in a
ten-month window around the switch (0.648, 95 per cent interval 0.52–0.81) and by
ten per cent over the full panel (0.901, 0.82–0.99). The correction needs one
number, recoverable from ordinary results data as a design effect.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: How much evidence a contest should collect before declaring a winner is a basic question of tournament design. Longer contests cost players, organisers and audiences time, while short contests let transitory shocks decide the result. Operational research has studied this trade-off closely, and it evaluates formats by their efficacy : the probability that the design identifies the stronger competitor ( Ryvkin & Ortmann, (2008) ; Lasek & Gagolewski, (2018) ; Sziklai et al., (2022) ) . Efficacy is almost always computed by simulation, and almost always under an assumption that is convenient rather than tested — that the trials a format aggregates, the games, sets or rounds, are independent. That assumption is not innocuous. When trials are serially correlated, a format carries fewer independent observations than its nominal length suggests, and the marginal trial carries less than the one before it. Both effects work in the same direction, and both are ignored by the independence benchmark. This paper measures the dependence directly and shows what it does to the arithmetic of format design. The answer is large and systematic: assuming independent trials overstates the efficacy lost by shortening a contest, by a factor of two in the setting we study and by more in longer formats. A twenty per cent cut in trials costs 10.6 per cent of discriminating power if trials are independent, but only 5.2 per cent once dependence is calibrated on the data, and only 3.5 per cent if the same cut is applied to a thirty-trial contest. Section 6 sets out the general correction; Sections 3 to 5 estimate the ingredients it needs from an implemented change in contest length. The empirical setting supplies what this literature usually lacks. Contest length is rarely varied while the rest of the game stays fixed, so efficacy is theorised and simulated far more often than it is measured. Professional Counter-Strike provides such a variation. The game is a team shooter, and its mechanics bear directly on the analysis, so we describe them briefly. Two teams of five play a sequence of short rounds on a map. One side, the terrorists, tries to plant a bomb at one of two sites and hold it until it detonates; the other, the counter-terrorists, tries to stop the plant, defuse the bomb, or survive the clock. A round lasts roughly two minutes and ends when one side achieves its objective or eliminates the other. Teams switch roles at half time, so each plays both sides of the map. One feature is central to the analysis: equipment is bought at the start of each round with money earned in earlier ones, so a team that wins a round can afford better weapons in the next and a team that loses often cannot. Round outcomes within a map are therefore not independent draws. Series are contested over one, three or five maps taken from a seven-map pool, which the two teams narrow beforehand by alternately banning and picking. The professional circuit is built on salaried teams and year-round tournaments, and it is large. Esports Earnings records $163 million in prize money across more than seven thousand Counter-Strike: Global Offensive tournaments since 2012, and a further $55 million under Counter-Strike 2 ( Esports Earnings, (2026) ) . Valve, the publisher, sanctions two Major championships a year with a prize pool of $1.25 million and thirty-two invited teams ( Valve Corporation, (2026) ) ; the final of the June 2026 Major drew a peak of 2.75 million concurrent viewers on Western streaming platforms alone ( HLTV.org, (2026) ) . Results, statistics and a weekly world ranking of teams are published by HLTV.org, founded in 2002 and the reference archive for the discipline. Our panel records 34,453 professional matches over four years. The competitive rules of this circuit changed in September 2023. Counter-Strike: Global Offensive, released in 2012, was replaced on 27 September 2023 by Counter-Strike 2, built on a new engine, and the competitive format moved from MR15 — fifteen rounds a half, first team to sixteen — to MR12, twelve rounds a half, first to thirteen, with a six-round overtime. Valve’s stated reason was that changes to the economy and to weapon balance had cut the number of uncontested rounds, so matches could be settled with fewer of them. The change was global and abrupt, every round is recorded, and the internal structure of a map lets us observe a contest whose length is fixed by rule rather than terminated by a stopping rule. Because MR12 arrived with the new engine, the setting offers a sharp transition rather than an isolated experiment in length. The change arrived with an explicit justification of exactly this kind, and with an explicit dissent. Announcing the move on 1 September 2023, Valve wrote that “over the past decade, we’ve shipped updates to the economy and weapon balance to trim the fat and reduce the number of uncontested rounds in a match of CS”, and concluded that “because of these changes, exciting competitive matches can be resolved with fewer rounds” ( Valve Corporation, (2023) ) . The evidence offered was about the composition of rounds rather than their number: teams reach a full buy in 73.3 per cent of non-pistol rounds after 2019 against 67.4 per cent before, and rounds in which one side cannot afford to contest have become rare. The claim is therefore not about duration but about information — each round is said to carry enough of it that twenty-four rounds now do the work of thirty. Professional players read the same change in the opposite direction. ropz, a two-time Major winner, predicted “even more random results”, on the grounds that pistol rounds, whose outcome can turn on the timing of a single headshot, would decide a larger share of every map ( HLTV.org, (2023) ) . Both sides are making a claim about how much one round reveals about which team is better, and in the debate that followed neither measured it. That quantity is estimable, and this paper estimates it. We measure how well a contest separates competitors by the residual-standardised ability slope, D = β / σ ε D=\beta/\sigma_{\varepsilon} : how far the expected outcome moves, in residual standard deviations, when the ability gap widens by one unit. The outcome is the favourite’s first-half round margin, a continuous variable measured over exactly fifteen or exactly twelve rounds, with no overtime and no endogenous stopping. Ability is a pre-match Elo rating updated on round shares rather than map results, so the scale does not depend on how many rounds a map contains. We begin with the calibration, which establishes the benchmark. Counter-Strike rounds are positively correlated through the in-game economy, and the over-dispersion of first-half scores implies an intra-class correlation of about 0.074 in both regimes. A fifteen-round half is therefore worth 7.35 independent draws, and twelve rounds of the same process 6.60. Cutting the contest by twenty per cent in rounds cuts it by ten per cent in information. The ratio of discriminations that length alone predicts is therefore 0.948, a decline of five per cent; had rounds been independent it would have been 0.894, a decline of eleven. The observed decline exceeds this benchmark. The discrimination ratio is 0.901 over the full 2022–2025 sample, with a cluster-bootstrap interval of [0.817, 0.991]. Within a ten-month window around the transition, which compares adjacent months rather than adjacent eras, it is 0.648 [0.519, 0.811]. The full-sample estimate is statistically indistinguishable from the mechanical benchmark (p = 0.28); the window estimate is not (p ¡ 0.001). Reweighting the new-format sample to the composition of the old moves the window estimate to 0.574, restricting to the 137 teams observed under both regimes gives 0.612, and adding team fixed effects strengthens the interaction rather than weakening it. Mechanical shortening predicts a decline of the observed sign, but it cannot account for the size of the decline observed among contemporaneous contests. The paper makes three contributions. We measure ability revelation around an implemented change in contest length rather than simulating one. We decompose the change into an ability slope and a residual-noise component, using a statistic taken unchanged from measurement theory, which is what lets the observed decline be compared with a calibrated mechanical benchmark instead of with zero. And we separate the arithmetic a shorter contest must produce from the part it cannot, by calibrating the round process rather than assuming independent trials. We introduce no new measure: the statistic is the ordinary discrimination parameter of test theory, and Section 2.2 records its prior identities. Section 2 places these contributions against the existing work on contest length, tournament design and the measurement of ability revelation. One limitation applies to every estimate reported below. MR12 arrived with a new engine, which changed movement, weapon behaviour, utility, the economy, the map pool and — as our own estimates show — the balance between the two sides. Nothing in the data separates the two changes, so the regime indicator is a joint indicator, and the results are effects of the transition rather than of round count alone. The mechanical benchmark bounds how much of the change contest shortening could produce; the excess cannot be assigned to any single accompanying mechanism. Section 2 reviews the literature. Section 3 describes the panel and how the round format is read off each map rather than assigned by date. Section 4 sets out the discrimination statistic, the calibration of the round process and the first-half design. Section 5 reports the estimates, narrows the comparison to contests played in the same weeks, and subjects the comparison to placebo splits, alternative samples and the measures of association that the literature conventionally reports. Section 6 concludes.

sections.heading: 2.1 Contest Length, Tournament Design and the Probability that the Stronger Competitor Wins
sections.text: The closest literature treats a contest as repeated noisy evidence about relative ability. Maisel ((1966)) and Gibbons et al. ((1978)) ask how many component games a best-of-k comparison needs before the better team wins with acceptable probability. Miles ((1984)) formalises scoring systems as symmetric sequential tests of the identity of the better player and compares their efficiency against the amount of play required. The comparative static is theirs: when component performances are informative but noisy, additional observations raise selection accuracy, by an amount that depends on the scoring and stopping rules. Applied work makes this proposition concrete and adds a qualification. Urban ((2013)) shows that longer playoff series need not favour the better team once the home-away sequence changes with series length. In tennis, Harris ((2016)) simulates a fall of 3.5 to 5 per cent in the stronger player’s win probability under no-ad and match-tiebreak scoring, and S.A. Kovalchik & Ingram ((2018)) report upset frequencies of 20 per cent under Fast4 against 13 per cent in best-of-three and 10 per cent in best-of-five; Simmonds & O’Donoghue ((2018)) reach the same conclusion. Dominicy et al. ((2013)) show that table tennis’s move from 21-point to 11-point sets makes victories against the odds more likely, and Percy ((2009)) compares badminton’s old and new scoring systems. These are the closest conceptual precedents for MR15 against MR12. They share a limitation: each translates assumed point- or rally-winning probabilities into counterfactual match outcomes, rather than estimating how an implemented change altered the empirical relation between ability and performance. A second literature evaluates formats by how reliably they select or rank competitors under noise. Ryvkin & Ortmann ((2008)) call the probability that the ex ante best player wins a tournament its predictive power. Lasek & Gagolewski ((2018)) compare league formats against latent team strengths, and Sziklai et al. ((2022)) rank knockout, group, multi-stage and Swiss designs under limited comparison budgets. Selecting a winner and ranking a field are distinct objectives, and the value of an extra contest turns on how comparisons are allocated, not on their number alone. Related work treats a single match as signal extraction. Skinner & Freeman ((2009)) ask how often the better soccer team wins and how misleading an observed result can be. Wolfson et al. ((2018)) measure how much a game reveals about team quality and how well it predicts later games. Lopez et al. ((2018)) separate latent strength from game-level noise in a Bayesian state-space model and simulate how postseason parity varies with series length. Holzmeister & Johannesson ((2025)) put a magnitude on the same decomposition at season length: across seven European football leagues and 7,240 matches they attribute roughly 40 per cent of the variation in performance relative to expectation to skill and 60 per cent to luck, which over a 38-match season leaves the identity of the champion sensitive to chance with probability 0.34 and the relegation places with probability 0.76. Their finding is the complement of ours in an instructive way: they hold the format fixed and show how little of the final table survives the noise even after a long season, whereas we hold the sport fixed and vary the length. Read together, the two say that the amount of play a format prescribes is a weak instrument for the reliability it delivers. We adopt this logic — evaluate a format by the information its outcomes carry about ability — but apply it within a single contest rather than across a tournament, and to observed rather than simulated variation. A separate strand supplies the design rather than the question. Apesteguia & Palacios-Huerta ((2010)) and Krumer ((2020)) study the penalty shoot-out precisely because its length and environment are fixed by regulation while the match around it is not, and Malueg & Yates ((2010)) test contest theory on the internal structure of a best-of-three rather than on who won it. The motivation for looking inside a match rather than at its result is documented on both sides: play is not independent of the running score ( Klaassen & Magnus, (2001) ; Lago-Peñas & Gómez-López, (2014) ) , and the match stops as soon as one side reaches the target. Section 4.2 applies that logic to the half of a Counter-Strike map.

sections.heading: 2.2 Measurement of Ability Revelation and the Remaining Gap
sections.text: The statistic is not ours. The measurement literature contains it under several names, and we adopt it in the form that literature established. Classical test theory defines reliability as the share of observed-score variance attributable to stable true-score differences ( Lord & Novick, (1968) ) . Signal-detection theory standardises the separation between two outcome distributions by their within-distribution noise ( Stanislaw & Todorov, (1999) ; Massof, (1987) ; DeCarlo, (2023) ) . In regression, signal variance relative to residual variance is Cohen’s f 2 f^{2} ( Cohen, (1988) ) . For the outcome M = α + β ​ S + ε M=\alpha+\beta S+\varepsilon , our D = β / σ ε D=\beta/\sigma_{\varepsilon} is the performance response to a one-unit rise in ability measured in residual standard deviations. When S S is standardised in a bivariate model D 2 D^{2} equals R 2 / ( 1 − R 2 ) R^{2}/(1-R^{2}) , reliability is D 2 / ( 1 + D 2 ) D^{2}/(1+D^{2}) , and for a contrast between two fixed ability levels β ​ Δ ​ S / σ ε \beta\Delta S/\sigma_{\varepsilon} is the discriminability d ′ d^{\prime} . The first of these identities is the signal-to-noise ratio of classical test theory, ρ / ( 1 − ρ ) \rho/(1-\rho) , whose equivalence with the information function of item response theory is established by Nicewander ((1993)) ; D D with a standardised S S is therefore also Cohen’s f f , and D D as we report it is f f expressed per 100 rating points rather than per standard deviation of ability. We keep D rather than R-squared because the latter also moves with the cross-sectional dispersion of ability, which differs across our two regimes. The statistic itself is standard; its application to a contest-format transition is not. The identity that matters most for the validity of what follows is with item response theory. Under a two-parameter normal-ogive model written in its latent-response form, the discrimination parameter of an item is exactly the slope of the latent-ability response divided by the residual standard deviation, a = λ / 1 − λ 2 a=\lambda/\sqrt{1-\lambda^{2}} for a standardised latent variable, and the information the item contributes to the ability estimate is proportional to its square ( Ferguson, (1949) ; Jordan & Spiess, (2019) ; Pavlech & Martinková, (2025) ) . Ferrando ((2012)) develops the same family of discrimination indices for the linear factor-analytic model, which is the case we are in: our outcome is continuous and our specification is linear, so the ratio β / σ ε \beta/\sigma_{\varepsilon} is the discrimination index of that model rather than an approximation to a binary-response one. Read a contest as an item that measures the latent ability of the competitors and D is that discrimination parameter, while the effective trial count of Section 4.2 is the information the contest carries. The correspondence is not an analogy constructed for this paper. Scale-invariance in the outcome, sensitivity to the units of the latent variable, and accumulation with the number of conditionally independent trials are properties established in that literature; we inherit them rather than assert them, and the interpretation of a cross-regime ratio of discriminations follows from them directly. The same ratio is what the tournament-design literature varies when it evaluates formats: the predictive power of Ryvkin & Ortmann ((2008)) is a monotone transformation of the gap in ability divided by the standard deviation of performance noise, so a format that raises D D is a format that more often selects the better competitor. The correction we apply for serial dependence is equally standard. The ratio of the observed variance of a half score to its binomial counterpart is the design effect of survey sampling, and the nominal number of rounds divided by it is the effective sample size ( Kish, (1965) ) . The same quantity appears in sports economics as the square of the Noll-Scully ratio of the actual to the idealised standard deviation of win percentages, whose dependence on the number of games played is well documented ( Owen, (2010) ) . Doria & Nalebuff ((2021)) make that dependence the object of study and construct measures of competitive balance that are invariant to season length, on the grounds that a measure moving mechanically with the amount of play cannot be compared across leagues that play different amounts. Our problem is the within-league form of theirs: because the treatment here is a change in the amount of play, a statistic that responds mechanically to length must be given a length-only benchmark before any residual movement can be read as substantive. Section 5.2 constructs that benchmark from the data rather than assuming independence, which is what the simulation literature on scoring systems typically assumes. Two clarifications keep the statistic where it belongs. First, discrimination in our sense is not the discriminatory power of contest theory. The parameter r of a Tullock contest success function, and the noise parameters that generalise it, govern how sensitively a modelled win probability responds to effort and are properties of an assumed functional form ( Amegashie, (2006) ; Jia, (2008) ) ; D is an estimated property of realised outcomes, and nothing in our design identifies r. Second, the empirical literature has measured objects of the same family without using this name. Lopez et al. ((2018)) and Wolfson et al. ((2018)) separate team strength from game-level noise; Heuer ((2020)) scores performance indicators by how much of the underlying team strength they recover net of statistical noise; Aoki et al. ((2017)) and Jerdee & Newman ((2024)) decompose outcomes into skill and luck, the latter with an explicit depth-of-competition parameter; Ben-Naim et al. ((2013)) work directly with the upset probability. Miles ((1984)) and its generalisation by Pollard ((2015)) evaluate scoring systems by the amount of play required to reach a given probability of identifying the better competitor, which is the same trade-off expressed as a cost rather than as a slope. We use D because it is estimable regime by regime from contests that were actually played and because its comparative static in length is sharp; we do not claim it improves on any of these. Evidence from implemented length changes remains scarce. Di Mattia & Krumer ((2026)) exploit a 2017 reform that cut round-robin matches per team in beach volleyball from three to two, and find no detectable change in favourite-win probability or in the alignment of final standings with initial strength. Theirs is the closest observed structural-change precedent, but the treatment varies the number of matches in a tournament stage rather than the number of repeated trials inside a single contest, and the outcome remains a win indicator. Esports research on tournament design largely imports methods built for traditional sport, and work on Counter-Strike concentrates on prediction, player valuation and in-game decisions. We found no scholarly analysis of the MR15-to-MR12 transition. The gap this paper fills is therefore not the proposition that shorter contests favour weaker competitors, which is well established. It is the measurement of ability revelation around an implemented transition, the separation of the ability-response and residual-noise components, and the comparison of the observed change with a mechanical benchmark calibrated on the effective number of rounds. Every element of the measurement apparatus is borrowed. What is new is that it is applied to a change in contest length that actually occurred, and that it is given a benchmark against which the estimate can fail.

sections.heading: 3.1 Source and Sample Construction
sections.text: The panel is assembled from HLTV.org, the reference results archive for professional Counter-Strike. It covers 1 January 2022 to 31 December 2025. The pipeline requests only URL families permitted by the site’s robots.txt: the paginated results archive, individual match pages, the weekly world-ranking archive and event pages. The date-filtered results view is disallowed, so the study window is located by binary search over the offset parameter of the unfiltered results list and then traversed page by page. Every page is stored in a compressed raw cache and every request is logged, so all downstream results can be re-derived without re-contacting the source. The crawl retrieved 34,453 match pages with no failures and no skipped observations. The window opens on 1 January 2022 rather than earlier for a substantive reason. Competitive play through 2020 and much of 2021 ran under pandemic restrictions: matches were played online, international travel was suspended for long stretches, and the circuit was segmented into regional brackets. Venue is a first-order determinant of play in this discipline — 18.1 per cent of our maps are at a LAN event and the indicator enters every map-level specification — and regional segmentation breaks the network of common opponents on which any rating recursion depends. 2022 is the first full year after the circuit returned to its normal calendar. The cost of that choice is that the rating recursion begins with the sample rather than before it, so ratings are least informative in the opening months of the panel. Section 5.3 documents the consequence and shows that removing those months moves the estimate away from one rather than towards it, so the full-sample figure is the conservative one. The unit of observation is a played map. A best-of-three series ending 2-0 contributes two observations, not three; the unplayed slot stays in the database but never enters the estimation sample. The raw panel contains 72,576 played maps and 17,820 unplayed slots across 34,453 matches, 2,547 teams and 2,451 events. Teams are identified by persistent site identifiers rather than names, so renamings and sponsor changes do not fragment a team’s history. Three exclusions define the estimation sample. We drop 1,446 walkover placeholders: a forfeit is recorded as a nominal 1-0 result on a map named “Default” with no round detail, and such records are not contests. We drop observations for which the pre-match world ranking of either team is unavailable, because the favourite cannot be defined; this affects 13,131 maps, overwhelmingly matches between teams outside the published ranking. We drop the small number of maps whose round format cannot be determined. The estimation sample contains 58,294 maps from 26,958 matches, 1,094 teams and 1,934 events. Specifications using the half decomposition also require the half-by-half score and the starting side to be recoverable and both teams to have at least twenty-five prior maps in the rating recursion, leaving 39,546 maps from 19,362 matches.

sections.heading: 3.2 Construction of the Key Variables
sections.text: The regime variable is the round format of the map: MR15, fifteen rounds per half and first to sixteen, or MR12, twelve rounds per half and first to thirteen. Assigning the format by calendar date relative to the engine release on 27 September 2023 would introduce substantial measurement error. Several leagues finished their previous-generation seasons after that date, and some final scores are observationally identical across regimes: a map ending 16-14 is either an MR15 regulation result or an MR12 map decided in the first overtime. The format is instead inferred from the scoreline of the map itself. The source reports the half-by-half score of every map in the form (10:5; 6:8), and a half is always played to completion, so the rounds contested in the first half identify the regime directly. Where the half string is missing we infer the format from unambiguous final scores, then from the observed format of other maps in the same event, and only as a last resort from the calendar; each observation records which rule applied. In the estimation window 97.96 per cent of maps are classified from the half structure, 1.92 per cent from the event majority, 0.04 per cent from the final score and 0.08 per cent from the calendar. A consistency filter discards half evidence that cannot generate the map’s own final score; five maps are affected. The favourite is the team with the better official world ranking in force before the match. We collected the weekly ranking archive in full for 29 November 2021 to 29 December 2025: 214 consecutive snapshots and 53,211 team-week observations, with roughly 235 to 265 ranked teams per snapshot. Snapshots are located by following each page’s own previous-week link rather than by generating Mondays, which picks up two irregular publication gaps a calendar-based iterator would miss. Matches are linked to rankings by an as-of join with a strict no-look-ahead rule: the applicable snapshot is the latest published on a strictly earlier calendar day, and each team is looked up in that snapshot only, so a team absent from it counts as unranked rather than carrying forward a stale rank. The realised lag runs from one to eight days, median four. Both teams are ranked for 81.9 per cent of maps. One institutional caveat is in order. The HLTV ranking is the consensus reference in the discipline, but it is not the ranking Valve uses: Major invitations and seeding run off the Valve Regional Standings. We use the HLTV ranking because it is published weekly, archived back to 2012 and covers far more teams than the invitation lists, and because it defines the favourite rather than allocating anything. Nothing in the design requires the ranking to be institutionally binding; Section 4.3 introduces a continuous rating estimated from the data itself, and the main results use that.

sections.heading: 4.1 A Measure of Performance Discrimination and the Prediction of Contest Length
sections.text: Let the outcome of a contest between two competitors be M = α + β ​ S + ε , M=\alpha+\beta S+\varepsilon, (1) where S is the difference in their ability and ε \varepsilon collects everything the contest itself contributes. We define the discrimination of the contest as D = β σ ε . D\;=\;\frac{\beta}{\sigma_{\varepsilon}}. (2) The two ingredients have plain readings. The slope β \beta is the signal : how far the expected outcome moves when one competitor is better than the other. The residual standard deviation σ ε \sigma_{\varepsilon} is the noise : how far realised outcomes scatter around that expectation when the ability gap is held fixed. In the estimates below the signal is 3.16 rounds per hundred rating points and the noise 5.42 rounds, so the contest is noisy: a single map is a weak signal of which team is better, which is why the question of how many rounds to play has force at all. The intercept α \alpha is a level term and plays no part in D D ; Section 4.2 explains why it is not zero. D answers the question a contest designer faces: by how many noise standard deviations does the expected outcome move when the ability gap widens by one unit. Two properties of D are relevant for what follows. D is invariant to the scale of the performance outcome, so first-half margins measured over fifteen and twelve rounds can be compared directly. It is not invariant to the units of ability, so the comparison requires S to stay on a common pre-match rating scale across regimes — which is why the rating recursion in Section 4.3 updates on round shares rather than map results. Unlike an R-squared or a correlation, D does not rise merely because the sample happens to contain a more dispersed set of ability gaps. That distinction is not hypothetical in this application: Section 5.5 shows the dispersion of the ability gap rising by a quarter across the transition, which is enough to reverse the sign of every standardised measure. What makes D D testable rather than merely descriptive is that it has a sharp comparative static in contest length. If a contest aggregates n n conditionally independent trials whose per-trial informativeness is unchanged, the signal accumulates in proportion to n n while the noise accumulates in proportion to n \sqrt{n} , so D ⁡ ( n ) ∝ n . D(n)\;\propto\;\sqrt{n}. (3) The prediction for a change in length is therefore a ratio of square roots of effective trial counts, and the effective count is estimable from the data. Section 4.2 estimates it. (The identities that make D D a standard object rather than one of our own are set out in Section 2.2 and not repeated here.) Let the stronger side win each round with probability p greater than one half. A race to sixteen over thirty regulation rounds resolves in favour of the stronger side more often than a race to thirteen over twenty-four, for every p, so the discrimination of the shorter contest is lower. The sign is unambiguous. The magnitude is not: it depends on how much independent information a single round carries. One question the design invites is why the half should be affected at all. It is because the half is not a fixed object across the two regimes: it is fifteen rounds under MR15 and twelve under MR12, so the treatment applies directly to the contest we measure. The magnitude then follows from ( 3 ). If rounds were independent, twelve of them would carry the information of twelve and fifteen the information of fifteen, and D D would fall by the factor 12 / 15 = 0.894 \sqrt{12/15}=0.894 — a decline of 10.6 per cent, not the 20 per cent that counting rounds suggests. Serial dependence moves the prediction closer to one rather than away from it, because the rounds that were removed were partly redundant; Section 4.2 measures how much, and Section 5.2 carries the calculation out. The point to carry forward is that the null of interest is a benchmark strictly between 0.894 and one, and never zero: nothing about the competitors has to change for a shorter contest to discriminate less.

sections.heading: 4.2 The Round-Generating Process and the First-Half Specification
sections.text: Rounds within a map are not independent. Equipment bought in one round persists into the next, so wins arrive in streaks. We model this as a beta-binomial process: the per-round win probability of a given map is drawn once from a Beta distribution centred on the team’s true value, and rounds are conditionally independent given that draw. The intra-class correlation is identified from the over-dispersion of first-half scores relative to the binomial benchmark, computed within forty fine strata of pre-match strength so that heterogeneity between matchups is not mistaken for correlation within a map: φ = Var ⁡ ( X ) N ​ p ¯ ​ ( 1 − p ¯ ) , ρ = φ − 1 N − 1 , N eff = N φ , \varphi\;=\;\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{N\,\bar{p}\,(1-\bar{p})},\qquad\rho\;=\;\frac{\varphi-1}{N-1},\qquad N_{\mathrm{eff}}\;=\;\frac{N}{\varphi}, (4) where X X is the favourite’s first-half round count, p ¯ \bar{p} its mean share and N N the number of rounds in the half. N eff N_{\mathrm{eff}} is the number of independent draws a half is worth, and the point prediction for the ratio of discriminations across regimes is N eff , 12 / N eff , 15 \sqrt{N_{\mathrm{eff},12}/N_{\mathrm{eff},15}} . The design exploits a feature of the rules. The first half of a map is a contest of exactly fifteen rounds under MR15 and exactly twelve under MR12. It has no stopping rule, no overtime and a continuous outcome, the round margin. It carries the same 12/15 length ratio as regulation play, 24 rounds against 30, without the truncation and the discrete threshold that make the map result an inefficient statistic. For each regime we estimate M i = α + β ​ S i + γ ​ 𝐶𝑇 i + δ m ⁡ ( i ) × side + ε i , M_{i}\;=\;\alpha+\beta S_{i}+\gamma\,\mathit{CT}_{i}+\delta_{m(i)\times\mathrm{side}}+\varepsilon_{i}, (5) where M i M_{i} is the favourite’s first-half round margin, S i S_{i} the pre-match rating difference, 𝐶𝑇 i \mathit{CT}_{i} an indicator for the favourite starting on the counter-terrorist side, and δ m ⁡ ( i ) × side \delta_{m(i)\times\mathrm{side}} a set of map fixed effects interacted with the side indicator, which absorbs the differing side balance of individual maps. Discrimination is β \beta divided by the residual standard deviation, and the statistic of interest is the cross-regime ratio. This follows a literature that isolates a sub-contest whose length and conditions are fixed by the rules, rather than analysing the match that contains it. Apesteguia & Palacios-Huerta ((2010)) and Krumer ((2020)) use the penalty shoot-out for that reason: the number of attempts is set by regulation, the environment is common to both sides, and the order is drawn by lot, none of which is true of the match around it. Malueg & Yates ((2010)) test contest theory on the internal structure of a best-of-three rather than on its outcome, and Magnus & Klaassen ((1999)) analyse a single named set of a tennis match as an object with its own properties. The reason for not using the whole match is documented from two directions: behaviour responds to the running score, so play recorded after the score moves is contaminated ( Klaassen & Magnus, (2001) ; Lago-Peñas & Gómez-López, (2014) ) , and the match itself ends the moment one side reaches the target, which censors the outcome and makes the amount of play a function of the state. The first half of a map is the counterpart of the shoot-out in this setting — fixed at fifteen rounds under MR15 and twelve under MR12, unable to end early, played by both teams under a side assignment we observe — with one addition: the outcome is a continuous margin rather than a binary result, which carries more information about strength ( S. Kovalchik, (2020) ; Lopez et al., (2018) ) . We follow the logic of these papers, not their question: none of them measures what happens when the length of the contest is changed. A second, pooled specification interacts ability with the regime indicator: M i = α + β ​ S i + θ ​ MR12 i + δ ⁡ ( S i × MR12 i ) + γ ​ 𝐶𝑇 i + λ map × side + μ t + ε i , M_{i}\;=\;\alpha+\beta S_{i}+\theta\,\mathit{MR12}_{i}+\delta\,(S_{i}\times\mathit{MR12}_{i})+\gamma\,\mathit{CT}_{i}+\lambda_{\mathrm{map}\times\mathrm{side}}+\mu_{t}+\varepsilon_{i}, (6) with μ t \mu_{t} a set of calendar fixed effects at the week or month level. The parameter of interest is δ \delta , the change in the ability slope; θ \theta is a nuisance term. The pooled form admits calendar and team fixed effects but forces the residual variance to be common across regimes, so the two specifications complement each other: the ratio of discriminations lets the noise term differ, the interaction lets us control time and teams.

sections.heading: 4.3 Measurement of Ability
sections.text: The published ranking is coarse: integer-valued, weekly, and covering only the leading two hundred and fifty or so teams. We build a continuous rating from the data. Ratings follow an Elo recursion with logistic scale 400 and all teams entering at 1500, updated after every map by r a ← r a + K ⁡ ( s a s a + s b − 1 1 + 10 ( r b − r a ) / 400 ) , r_{a}\;\leftarrow\;r_{a}+K\!\left(\frac{s_{a}}{s_{a}+s_{b}}-\frac{1}{1+10^{(r_{b}-r_{a})/400}}\right), (7) where s a s_{a} and s b s_{b} are rounds won. Two features of this recursion matter. The update uses the round share rather than the map result, so it does not depend on how many rounds a map contains and ratings estimated under MR12 sit on the same scale as ratings estimated under MR15. And every map is scored with the ratings both teams carried into it, so the regressor is strictly pre-determined. The implementation is deliberately simple. Maps are processed in chronological order by date, then match identifier, then map number. There is no seasonal decay, no roster-change adjustment and no special handling of inactive teams. New teams enter at the common prior and are excluded from estimation until they have twenty-five prior maps, which is also required of their opponent. Walkovers carry no round information and do not update ratings. We fixed the step size K = 24 before estimating any reported specification, but chose it with reference to in-sample predictive fit rather than a pre-registered rule, so Table 5 reports the main statistic across K in {12, 18, 24, 32, 48}.

sections.heading: 4.4 Identification
sections.text: The round format did not change in isolation. MR12 arrived with a new engine, which altered movement, weapon behaviour, utility, the economy, the map pool and, as Section 5.5 documents, the balance between the two sides. Nothing reachable under the source’s access rules carries an independent per-match marker of the engine, and the handful of leagues that continued under MR15 after the release is the only variation separating the two. The regime indicator is therefore a joint indicator for the format change and the engine change, and the estimates are effects of the transition, not of round count net of everything else. This has an implication for how the results should be interpreted. If the observed change in discrimination matched the magnitude implied by the reduction in rounds alone, that would be consistent with a pure length mechanism but would not prove one, since an engine effect of zero is not testable here. If the observed change were substantially larger, the excess would have to come from the accompanying changes. Section 5.3 finds the second pattern. What the design does deliver is comparability along two dimensions that would otherwise be fatal. The first-half outcome fixes contest length by rule rather than by the state of play, so the comparison is not contaminated by the endogenous stopping rule of the map. And the transition-window specifications hold calendar time fixed, which removes the confound of a professional scene that changed considerably between 2022 and 2025. Neither device removes the engine change.

sections.heading: 4.5 Inference
sections.text: Maps of the same series are not independent, so we cluster standard errors at the match level throughout. The discrimination ratio is a non-linear function of two fits estimated on disjoint samples, so we obtain its sampling distribution by a cluster bootstrap over matches, drawn separately within each regime, with 1,000 replications for the headline estimates, 600 for the regime-specific levels of D D plotted in Figure 1 , 400 for the remaining rows of Table 4 and 300 for the alternative measures of Table 7 ; the smaller counts are a concession to the cost of refitting eight statistics per draw, and doubling them moves no reported interval endpoint by more than 0.005. Reported p-values are two-sided bootstrap probabilities of a ratio at least as far from the stated null as the estimate. The calibrated benchmark of Section 5.2 is itself estimated, but with a bootstrap interval of [0.946, 0.949] it is treated as known when the observed ratios are tested against it.

It is not a bound in either direction: nothing in the design makes the full-sample number a floor under the true effect, and if the professional scene changed in ways that raised discrimination over 2024–2025 it could equally overstate it. sections.heading: 5.2 What the Change Should Have Cost
sections.text: The question has an exact answer, and reaching it takes two steps: first what a shorter contest costs when its rounds are independent, then how much of that cost survives the fact that they are not. Both steps are standard; only the second requires data. Step 1: if rounds were independent. Write the margin as an advantage plus luck. The advantage points the same way in every round and therefore accumulates in proportion to the number of rounds: at a per-round win probability of 0.55, fifteen rounds give an expected margin of 15 × ( 0.55 − 0.45 ) = 1.50 15\times(0.55-0.45)=1.50 rounds and twelve give 1.20. Luck points either way and therefore partly cancels: in the sum of N N independent deviations the cross-terms average to zero, so it is the squared deviations that add and the standard deviation grows as N \sqrt{N} rather than as N N . Over fifteen rounds the standard deviation of the margin is 2 ​ 15 × 0.55 × 0.45 = 3.85 2\sqrt{15\times 0.55\times 0.45}=3.85 rounds; over twelve it is 3.45. The signal-to-noise ratio is therefore 1.50 / 3.85 = 0.389 1.50/3.85=0.389 against 1.20 / 3.45 = 0.348 1.20/3.45=0.348 , and their ratio is D ⁡ ( 12 ) D ⁡ ( 15 ) = 0.1 × 12 / 12 0.1 × 15 / 15 = 12 15 = 12 15 = 0.894 . \frac{D(12)}{D(15)}\;=\;\frac{0.1\times 12/\sqrt{12}}{0.1\times 15/\sqrt{15}}\;=\;\frac{\sqrt{12}}{\sqrt{15}}\;=\;\sqrt{\tfrac{12}{15}}\;=\;0.894. Neither the square-root law nor its use in evaluating formats is new. It is the content of the Spearman-Brown prophecy formula ( Spearman, (1910) ; Brown, (1910) ; Lord & Novick, (1968) ) , under which lengthening a test raises its reliability and its discrimination with the square root of its length, and it is the mechanism behind the predictive power of Ryvkin & Ortmann ((2008)) . (11) Three remarks on this number, since it is the paper’s main construction. First, the three candidate predictions should be stated together rather than contrasted with a straw man. sections.heading: 5.4 What the Change Means for Who Wins
sections.text: Ratios of discriminations are the right object for testing and the wrong object for a rulebook. This subsection translates them into units an organiser can use. It is an illustration computed from the fitted model rather than a further estimate, and two things about it need stating before the numbers. What the quantity is. Under the specification of Section 4.1 the margin is normal with mean α + β ​ S \alpha+\beta S and standard deviation σ ε \sigma_{\varepsilon} , so Pr ⁡ ( M > 0 ) = Φ ⁡ ( α + β ​ S σ ε ) = Φ ⁡ ( D ​ S ) , \Pr(M>0)\;=\;\Phi\!\left(\frac{\alpha+\beta S}{\sigma_{\varepsilon}}\right)\;=\;\Phi(DS), (12) where the second equality sets the level term to the value at which equally rated teams split the half evenly. A continuous approximation, however, cannot be read as the probability of winning a twelve-round half, because such a half can end six–six and 13.9 per cent of them do; a fifteen-round half cannot be drawn. The quantity Φ ⁡ ( D ​ S ) \Phi(DS) is instead the favourite’s share of the decision — a win counted as one and a draw as one half — which is the only version of the statistic that is comparable across a format that admits draws and one that does not. That reading is not an assertion. Evaluating the calibrated beta-binomial of Section 4.2 at the same rating gaps gives the favourite a share of 53.6, 57.2, 60.7 and 63.2 per cent at gaps of 20, 40, 60 and 74 rating points, against 53.7, 57.4, 61.0 and 63.5 from Φ ⁡ ( D ​ S ) \Phi(DS) ; the discrete and the continuous versions agree to within half a point across the range. Table 5 reports both, so that the outright-win and draw probabilities are visible alongside the share. One caveat: at the window’s matchups the beta-binomial puts 15.8 per cent of MR12 halves level against 13.9 per cent observed, so it somewhat overstates the draw mass and correspondingly understates outright wins. Where the numbers are evaluated. The rating gaps in Table 5 are quantiles of the gap distribution actually observed in the window, not round numbers. The median gap is 19.5 rating points, the 75th percentile 39.7, the 90th 59.9 and the 95th 73.6; fewer than one map in a hundred exceeds 100 points and the largest gap in the window is 153. Evaluating the expression at 200 or 300 points, as an earlier draft of this section did, is extrapolation beyond the support of the data and we do not report it. Read that way, Table 5 and Figure 4 say three things. First, what shortening alone can explain is small in these units. Across the observed range of gaps the length-only benchmark costs the favourite at most 1.3 points of share, and at the median gap about 0.3. An organiser choosing between twelve and fifteen rounds, and right in believing nothing else would move, would be trading roughly one decision in three hundred at a typical matchup for a fifth of the playing time. On those terms the trade is defensible. Second, the change that occurred is an order of magnitude larger. At the 90th percentile of the gap the favourite’s share falls from 66.8 to 61.0 per cent, and at the median from 55.7 to 53.7. The largest gap anywhere in the window, 153 points, gives 10.3 points of share. These are not dramatic numbers, and it is better to state them plainly than to reach for a more impressive gap that the data do not contain: what the transition cost the better team, at the matchups professional Counter-Strike actually produces, is on the order of two to six points of decision share. Third, the effect is hump-shaped in the rating gap and the observed range sits on its rising limb. Between evenly matched teams the outcome is near a coin flip under any format; the cost of a shorter contest grows with the gap over the entire range present in the data. Whether it would turn down again at the very large gaps where the favourite wins under any format is a property of the functional form, not something the window can show. Within the calibrated model, lengthening the half cannot recover the window’s decline; outside it, the honest statement is only that the required lengthening is large and that recovering discrimination across contests — more maps in a series — is a cheaper instrument than lengthening one.

sections.heading: 5.6 A Coincident Change: Side Balance
sections.text: The same estimates identify a structural change arriving with the same transition. Under MR15, starting a half on the counter-terrorist side was worth 1.06 additional rounds (standard error 0.10). Under MR12 the figure is − 0.01 -0.01 (standard error 0.06), indistinguishable from zero: the sides were balanced. Side advantage cancels over a full map, since each team plays each side once, but it is a large source of within-half variation, and the side indicator and its interaction with map fixed effects absorb it throughout. The result matters for interpretation rather than for the estimates. It shows directly that the round-generating environment changed at the transition, not only its length, and it is the identification problem of Section 4.4 made visible in the estimates themselves. At least one accompanying change is large and measurable; there may be others that are not.

sections.heading: 5.7 Limitations
sections.text: Four limitations bound the estimates. The first is identification: the round format changed simultaneously with the engine, no measurement here separates them, and the regime indicator is a joint indicator. We do not claim that shortening the contest caused the observed fall in discrimination. We claim that the fall has the sign the length mechanism predicts, that its magnitude in the window comparisons exceeds what length alone can deliver under a calibrated round process, and that at least one accompanying change, the equalisation of side balance, is visible in the same estimates. The translation into win probabilities in Section 5.4 is an illustration computed from the fitted model, and inherits both that limitation and the approximation error of the beta-binomial. The second is that the window narrows calendar distance without eliminating it. Inside the ten months the two formats are still largely sequential, and only three of forty-three weeks contain both; the strictly contemporaneous comparison exists but rests on 483 maps and its interval covers no change. Anything specific to the autumn of 2023 and distinct from the format — a patch, a break in the calendar, a shift in which tier of event was running — is therefore not differenced out. What the design rules out is an era effect accumulating over years, not a shock lasting a season. The third is selection. The window comparison rests on a non-random set of MR15 observations: leagues that chose to finish their seasons under the old rules. Reweighting on observables and restricting to teams present in both regimes do not overturn the contrast, but selection on unobservables cannot be ruled out. The fourth is coverage and measurement. The ranking that defines the favourite covers roughly the leading two hundred and fifty teams, so the results are conditional on both teams being ranked and say nothing about the long tail of professional play. The rating recursion makes no adjustment for roster changes, which are frequent here and add classical measurement error to the ability regressor; that error attenuates the slopes in both regimes.

sections.heading: 6 The Bias from Assuming Independent Trials
sections.text: The estimates above were built to test one rule change. The correction they rest on is general, and this section states it in the form the tournament-design literature can use. Let a format aggregate N N trials whose pairwise correlation is ρ \rho . The effective number of independent trials is N eff ​ ( N , ρ ) = N 1 + ( N − 1 ) ​ ρ , N_{\text{eff}}(N,\rho)\;=\;\frac{N}{1+(N-1)\rho}, (13) and discriminating power grows with its square root, so the efficacy of a format of length N 2 N_{2} relative to one of length N 1 N_{1} is N eff ​ ( N 2 , ρ ) / N eff ​ ( N 1 , ρ ) \sqrt{N_{\text{eff}}(N_{2},\rho)/N_{\text{eff}}(N_{1},\rho)} rather than N 2 / N 1 \sqrt{N_{2}/N_{1}} . Setting ρ = 0 \rho=0 recovers the independence benchmark that simulation studies impose by construction. The two expressions diverge sharply, and in a direction that matters for policy. Under independence, cutting a format by twenty per cent always costs 10.6 per cent of discriminating power, whatever the format’s length: the ratio 0.8 \sqrt{0.8} does not depend on N N . Under dependence it depends on N N strongly, because the trials removed from a long format were the ones carrying least new information. At the intra-class correlation we estimate, ρ ^ = 0.074 \hat{\rho}=0.074 , a twenty per cent cut costs 6.3 per cent at ten trials, 5.2 per cent at fifteen, 3.5 per cent at thirty and 2.1 per cent at sixty. The independence assumption therefore overstates the cost of shortening by a factor of 1.7 at ten trials and 5.1 at sixty. The independence figure is 10.6 per cent in every row because 0.8 \sqrt{0.8} does not depend on N N ; the calibrated figure falls with length, because the trials a long format gives up were the ones adding least. The final column is the ratio of the two, that is, the factor by which an independence-based simulation overstates the cost of shortening. Two implications follow for applied work. First, published efficacy comparisons between formats of different length are biased against the shorter format, and the bias grows with the length of the formats compared. A simulation that treats games in a best-of-seven series, or matches in a round-robin, as independent will report a larger advantage for the longer design than the data support. The direction is not ambiguous: dependence always moves the comparison towards no change, because N eff N_{\text{eff}} is concave in N N . Second, the correction is cheap to apply. It needs one number, ρ \rho , and that number is recoverable from ordinary results data without observing the trials’ dependence structure directly: the ratio of the observed variance of a format’s score to its binomial counterpart is the design effect φ = 1 + ( N − 1 ) ​ ρ \varphi=1+(N-1)\rho of survey sampling ( Kish, (1965) ) , and φ \sqrt{\varphi} is the Noll–Scully ratio already familiar in this literature ( Owen, (2010) ; Doria & Nalebuff, (2021) ) . Section 4.2 shows the estimation in full; it requires only scores, and it must be computed conditional on the strength gap, since unequal pairings otherwise enter as spurious dependence. A caution bounds both implications. Equation ( 13 ) assumes exchangeable trials, so a single ρ \rho describes every pair. That is a reasonable approximation over the twelve- and fifteen-trial formats on which we calibrate it, and it is what makes the ceiling N eff → 1 / ρ N_{\text{eff}}\to 1/\rho appear as N N grows; but nothing in our data speaks to whether trials fifty apart are correlated like trials one apart. Where dependence decays with distance — plausible in long seasons, less so within a single match — the correction remains valid in direction and should be recalibrated in magnitude.

sections.heading: 7 Concluding Remarks
sections.text: Efficacy comparisons between tournament formats of different length are biased when the trials a format aggregates are treated as independent, and this paper measures the bias. Because trials are serially correlated, a format carries N / [ 1 + ( N − 1 ) ​ ρ ] N/[1+(N-1)\rho] effective trials rather than N N , so the cost of shortening is smaller than the independence benchmark implies and the gap widens with the length of the formats compared: a twenty per cent cut costs 10.6 per cent of discriminating power under independence, 5.2 per cent at the correlation we estimate, and 2.1 per cent in a sixty-trial format. The correction needs a single parameter, and that parameter is recoverable from ordinary results data as a design effect. The ingredients come from an implemented change. The transition to Counter-Strike 2 and MR12 was accompanied by a fall in how sharply map outcomes track ability, and in the ten months around the switch that fall was larger than the calibrated model predicts. We do not attribute it to the round count: format and engine changed together, and Section 5.7 sets out what that leaves unidentified. Fifteen rounds carry the equivalent of 7.35 independent observations and twelve of the same process 6.60, so shortening on its own predicts a five per cent fall in the ability slope per unit of residual noise. We estimate ten per cent across 2022–2025, which is consistent with that benchmark, and thirty-five per cent in the window around the transition, which is not. The statistic behind these numbers is the ordinary discrimination parameter of measurement theory; what the paper adds is the benchmark it is measured against. One implication follows for the evaluation of format changes. Shortening a contest cannot be assessed from duration, nor from the nominal number of trials removed: the informative object is how much ability-relevant information survives per unit of play, which depends on serial dependence in the scoring process as much as on the number of trials — a rule change that halves the rounds does not halve the evidence. The estimates measure a bundled transition, not the round count alone, because MR12 arrived with Counter-Strike 2. Two extensions would separate them. Formats within the discipline vary in length while leaving the round process untouched, and other esports have changed series length without changing the game; either provides the clean contrast this setting lacks. Whether the sharp contemporaneous decline persists as teams adapt to the new engine is a question the next three seasons of the same panel will answer.

sections.heading: 8 Data Collection and Sample Construction
sections.text: This appendix documents how the panel was assembled, in enough detail for the procedure to be repeated from the public source.

sections.heading: A.1 Source and crawl
sections.text: All records come from HLTV.org, the reference results archive for professional Counter-Strike. Three page families are used. Match pages carry the date, the event, the two teams, the series format, the per-map scores and the link to each map’s statistics page. Map statistics pages carry the half-by-half score in the form (a : b ; c : d) , from which the first-half score and the starting side of each team are recovered. Ranking pages carry the weekly world ranking and its points, published each Monday, from which the pre-match ranking of both teams is taken by the snapshot in force on the date of the match. Pages were retrieved in chronological order of match identifier, one request at a time with a fixed delay between requests, and cached to disk before parsing, so that parsing is reproducible without re-crawling. The raw page cache is part of the replication package. No page was retrieved more than once except where a parse error required it.

sections.heading: A.2 Determining the round format
sections.text: The round format is the treatment, so it is read off each map rather than assigned by date. Two signals are used, in that order of priority. First, the half-score structure: a map whose two halves sum to fifteen rounds each is MR15, and one whose halves sum to twelve is MR12. Second, where half scores are missing, the regulation total: thirty rounds implies MR15 and twenty-four implies MR12. Maps for which neither signal is available, or whose signals conflict, are flagged and dropped. The source also carries a game-version field, but it is not an independent third signal and we do not use it as one: in these records the version is itself inferred from the round format, so treating it as corroboration would be circular. This is the same point made in Section 3.2 — the panel contains no marker of the engine that is independent of the format — and it is one reason the two changes cannot be separated. Reading the format from the map rather than the calendar matters because the transition was staggered. Leagues already in progress on 1 September 2023 finished their seasons under MR15 while new events started under MR12, and a small number of events ran the two formats in parallel. It is precisely this staggering that creates the ten-month window on which the paper’s preferred comparison rests; a date-based assignment would have destroyed it.

sections.heading: A.3 Exclusions
sections.text: Three exclusions define the estimation sample. Walkovers and forfeits are dropped (1,446 records): a forfeit appears as a nominal 1–0 result on a map named “Default” with no round detail, and is not a contest. Maps for which the pre-match world ranking of either team is unavailable are dropped (13,131 records), because the favourite cannot be defined; these are overwhelmingly matches between teams outside the published ranking. Maps whose round format cannot be determined are dropped. What remains is the estimation sample of 58,294 maps from 26,958 matches, 1,094 teams and 1,934 events. Specifications that use the half decomposition impose two further requirements: the half-by-half score and the starting side must be recoverable, and both teams must already have at least twenty-five maps in the rating recursion. This leaves the 39,546 maps from 19,362 matches described in Table 1 .

sections.heading: A.4 Variables
sections.text: The favourite is the better-ranked team at the time of the match; ties in rank are broken by ranking points and, failing that, the map is dropped. The first-half margin M i M_{i} is the favourite’s first-half rounds minus the underdog’s. The starting side is the favourite’s side in the first half, read from the half-score structure. The rating gap S i S_{i} is the difference in pre-match round-share Elo, favourite minus underdog, expressed per hundred points; the recursion is described in Section 4.3 and its step size is examined in Table 6 .

sections.text: The collection pipeline, the parsers, the database schema and the estimation code are available in a replication package together with the compressed page cache, so that every number in the paper can be reproduced without contacting the source site. The package documents the crawl order, the request pacing and the classification rules applied to each map.
