We show that this assumption systematically overstates what shortening a contest costs, and we measure the correction. When trials are serially correlated, a format carries N / [ 1 + ( N − 1 ) ​ ρ ] N/[1+(N-1)\rho] effective trials rather than N N , so a twenty per cent cut costs 10.6 per cent of discriminating power under independence but only 5.2 per cent at the correlation we estimate, and only 2.1 per cent in a sixty-trial format. The ingredients are estimated from an implemented change in contest length: in September 2023 professional Counter-Strike cut regulation rounds per map from thirty to twenty-four. Across 72,576 maps we measure discrimination as the ability slope over the residual standard deviation on the first half of a map, a contest fixed by rule at fifteen or twelve rounds with no stopping rule. Against the calibrated benchmark of 0.948, discrimination falls by thirty-five per cent in a ten-month window around the switch (0.648, 95 per cent interval 0.52–0.81) and by ten per cent over the full panel (0.901, 0.82–0.99). The correction needs one number, recoverable from ordinary results data as a design effect. keywords Tournament design, Contest length, Efficacy, Effective sample size, Competitive balance, Esports pacs [ 1 Introduction How much evidence a contest should collect before declaring a winner is a basic question of tournament design. Longer contests cost players, organisers and audiences time, while short contests let transitory shocks decide the result. Operational research has studied this trade-off closely, and it evaluates formats by their efficacy : the probability that the design identifies the stronger competitor ( Ryvkin & Ortmann, (2008) ; Lasek & Gagolewski, (2018) ; Sziklai et al., (2022) ) . Efficacy is almost always computed by simulation, and almost always under an assumption that is convenient rather than tested — that the trials a format aggregates, the games, sets or rounds, are independent. That assumption is not innocuous. When trials are serially correlated, a format carries fewer independent observations than its nominal length suggests, and the marginal trial carries less than the one before it. Both effects work in the same direction, and both are ignored by the independence benchmark. This paper measures the dependence directly and shows what it does to the arithmetic of format design. The answer is large and systematic: assuming independent trials overstates the efficacy lost by shortening a contest, by a factor of two in the setting we study and by more in longer formats. A twenty per cent cut in trials costs 10.6 per cent of discriminating power if trials are independent, but only 5.2 per cent once dependence is calibrated on the data, and only 3.5 per cent if the same cut is applied to a thirty-trial contest. Section 6 sets out the general correction; Sections 3 to 5 estimate the ingredients it needs from an implemented change in contest length. The empirical setting supplies what this literature usually lacks. Contest length is rarely varied while the rest of the game stays fixed, so efficacy is theorised and simulated far more often than it is measured. Professional Counter-Strike provides such a variation. The game is a team shooter, and its mechanics bear directly on the analysis, so we describe them briefly. Two teams of five play a sequence of short rounds on a map. One side, the terrorists, tries to plant a bomb at one of two sites and hold it until it detonates; the other, the counter-terrorists, tries to stop the plant, defuse the bomb, or survive the clock. A round lasts roughly two minutes and ends when one side achieves its objective or eliminates the other. Teams switch roles at half time, so each plays both sides of the map. One feature is central to the analysis: equipment is bought at the start of each round with money earned in earlier ones, so a team that wins a round can afford better weapons in the next and a team that loses often cannot. Round outcomes within a map are therefore not independent draws. Series are contested over one, three or five maps taken from a seven-map pool, which the two teams narrow beforehand by alternately banning and picking. The professional circuit is built on salaried teams and year-round tournaments, and it is large. Esports Earnings records $163 million in prize money across more than seven thousand Counter-Strike: Global Offensive tournaments since 2012, and a further $55 million under Counter-Strike 2 ( Esports Earnings, (2026) ) . Valve, the publisher, sanctions two Major championships a year with a prize pool of $1.25 million and thirty-two invited teams ( Valve Corporation, (2026) ) ; the final of the June 2026 Major drew a peak of 2.75 million concurrent viewers on Western streaming platforms alone ( HLTV.org, (2026) ) . Results, statistics and a weekly world ranking of teams are published by HLTV.org, founded in 2002 and the reference archive for the discipline. Our panel records 34,453 professional matches over four years. The competitive rules of this circuit changed in September 2023. Counter-Strike: Global Offensive, released in 2012, was replaced on 27 September 2023 by Counter-Strike 2, built on a new engine, and the competitive format moved from MR15 — fifteen rounds a half, first team to sixteen — to MR12, twelve rounds a half, first to thirteen, with a six-round overtime. Valve’s stated reason was that changes to the economy and to weapon balance had cut the number of uncontested rounds, so matches could be settled with fewer of them. The change was global and abrupt, every round is recorded, and the internal structure of a map lets us observe a contest whose length is fixed by rule rather than terminated by a stopping rule. Because MR12 arrived with the new engine, the setting offers a sharp transition rather than an isolated experiment in length. The change arrived with an explicit justification of exactly this kind, and with an explicit dissent. Announcing the move on 1 September 2023, Valve wrote that “over the past decade, we’ve shipped updates to the economy and weapon balance to trim the fat and reduce the number of uncontested rounds in a match of CS”, and concluded that “because of these changes, exciting competitive matches can be resolved with fewer rounds” ( Valve Corporation, (2023) ) . The evidence offered was about the composition of rounds rather than their number: teams reach a full buy in 73.3 per cent of non-pistol rounds after 2019 against 67.4 per cent before, and rounds in which one side cannot afford to contest have become rare. The claim is therefore not about duration but about information — each round is said to carry enough of it that twenty-four rounds now do the work of thirty. Professional players read the same change in the opposite direction. ropz, a two-time Major winner, predicted “even more random results”, on the grounds that pistol rounds, whose outcome can turn on the timing of a single headshot, would decide a larger share of every map ( HLTV.org, (2023) ) . Both sides are making a claim about how much one round reveals about which team is better, and in the debate that followed neither measured it. That quantity is estimable, and this paper estimates it. We measure how well a contest separates competitors by the residual-standardised ability slope, D = β / σ ε D=\beta/\sigma_{\varepsilon} : how far the expected outcome moves, in residual standard deviations, when the ability gap widens by one unit. The outcome is the favourite’s first-half round margin, a continuous variable measured over exactly fifteen or exactly twelve rounds, with no overtime and no endogenous stopping. Ability is a pre-match Elo rating updated on round shares rather than map results, so the scale does not depend on how many rounds a map contains. We begin with the calibration, which establishes the benchmark. Counter-Strike rounds are positively correlated through the in-game economy, and the over-dispersion of first-half scores implies an intra-class correlation of about 0.074 in both regimes. A fifteen-round half is therefore worth 7.35 independent draws, and twelve rounds of the same process 6.60. Cutting the contest by twenty per cent in rounds cuts it by ten per cent in information. The ratio of discriminations that length alone predicts is therefore 0.948, a decline of five per cent; had rounds been independent it would have been 0.894, a decline of eleven. The observed decline exceeds this benchmark. The discrimination ratio is 0.901 over the full 2022–2025 sample, with a cluster-bootstrap interval of [0.817, 0.991]. Within a ten-month window around the transition, which compares adjacent months rather than adjacent eras, it is 0.648 [0.519, 0.811]. The full-sample estimate is statistically indistinguishable from the mechanical benchmark (p = 0.28); the window estimate is not (p ¡ 0.001). Reweighting the new-format sample to the composition of the old moves the window estimate to 0.574, restricting to the 137 teams observed under both regimes gives 0.612, and adding team fixed effects strengthens the interaction rather than weakening it. Mechanical shortening predicts a decline of the observed sign, but it cannot account for the size of the decline observed among contemporaneous contests. The paper makes three contributions. We measure ability revelation around an implemented change in contest length rather than simulating one. We decompose the change into an ability slope and a residual-noise component, using a statistic taken unchanged from measurement theory, which is what lets the observed decline be compared with a calibrated mechanical benchmark instead of with zero. And we separate the arithmetic a shorter contest must produce from the part it cannot, by calibrating the round process rather than assuming independent trials. We introduce no new measure: the statistic is the ordinary discrimination parameter of test theory, and Section 2.2 records its prior identities. Section 2 places these contributions against the existing work on contest length, tournament design and the measurement of ability revelation. One limitation applies to every estimate reported below. MR12 arrived with a new engine, which changed movement, weapon behaviour, utility, the economy, the map pool and — as our own estimates show — the balance between the two sides. Nothing in the data separates the two changes, so the regime indicator is a joint indicator, and the results are effects of the transition rather than of round count alone. The mechanical benchmark bounds how much of the change contest shortening could produce; the excess cannot be assigned to any single accompanying mechanism. Section 2 reviews the literature. Section 3 describes the panel and how the round format is read off each map rather than assigned by date. Section 4 sets out the discrimination statistic, the calibration of the round process and the first-half design. Section 5 reports the estimates, narrows the comparison to contests played in the same weeks, and subjects the comparison to placebo splits, alternative samples and the measures of association that the literature conventionally reports. Section 6 concludes. 2 Related Literature 2.1 Contest Length, Tournament Design and the Probability that the Stronger Competitor Wins The closest literature treats a contest as repeated noisy evidence about relative ability. Maisel ((1966)) and Gibbons et al. ((1978)) ask how many component games a best-of-k comparison needs before the better team wins with acceptable probability. Miles ((1984)) formalises scoring systems as symmetric sequential tests of the identity of the better player and compares their efficiency against the amount of play required. The comparative static is theirs: when component performances are informative but noisy, additional observations raise selection accuracy, by an amount that depends on the scoring and stopping rules. Applied work makes this proposition concrete and adds a qualification. Urban ((2013)) shows that longer playoff series need not favour the better team once the home-away sequence changes with series length. In tennis, Harris ((2016)) simulates a fall of 3.5 to 5 per cent in the stronger player’s win probability under no-ad and match-tiebreak scoring, and S.A. Kovalchik & Ingram ((2018)) report upset frequencies of 20 per cent under Fast4 against 13 per cent in best-of-three and 10 per cent in best-of-five; Simmonds & O’Donoghue ((2018)) reach the same conclusion. Dominicy et al. ((2013)) show that table tennis’s move from 21-point to 11-point sets makes victories against the odds more likely, and Percy ((2009)) compares badminton’s old and new scoring systems. These are the closest conceptual precedents for MR15 against MR12. They share a limitation: each translates assumed point- or rally-winning probabilities into counterfactual match outcomes, rather than estimating how an implemented change altered the empirical relation between ability and performance. A second literature evaluates formats by how reliably they select or rank competitors under noise. Ryvkin & Ortmann ((2008)) call the probability that the ex ante best player wins a tournament its predictive power. Lasek & Gagolewski ((2018)) compare league formats against latent team strengths, and Sziklai et al. ((2022)) rank knockout, group, multi-stage and Swiss designs under limited comparison budgets. Selecting a winner and ranking a field are distinct objectives, and the value of an extra contest turns on how comparisons are allocated, not on their number alone. Related work treats a single match as signal extraction. Skinner & Freeman ((2009)) ask how often the better soccer team wins and how misleading an observed result can be. Wolfson et al. ((2018)) measure how much a game reveals about team quality and how well it predicts later games. Lopez et al. ((2018)) separate latent strength from game-level noise in a Bayesian state-space model and simulate how postseason parity varies with series length. Holzmeister & Johannesson ((2025)) put a magnitude on the same decomposition at season length: across seven European football leagues and 7,240 matches they attribute roughly 40 per cent of the variation in performance relative to expectation to skill and 60 per cent to luck, which over a 38-match season leaves the identity of the champion sensitive to chance with probability 0.34 and the relegation places with probability 0.76. Their finding is the complement of ours in an instructive way: they hold the format fixed and show how little of the final table survives the noise even after a long season, whereas we hold the sport fixed and vary the length. Read together, the two say that the amount of play a format prescribes is a weak instrument for the reliability it delivers. We adopt this logic — evaluate a format by the information its outcomes carry about ability — but apply it within a single contest rather than across a tournament, and to observed rather than simulated variation. A separate strand supplies the design rather than the question. Apesteguia & Palacios-Huerta ((2010)) and Krumer ((2020)) study the penalty shoot-out precisely because its length and environment are fixed by regulation while the match around it is not, and Malueg & Yates ((2010)) test contest theory on the internal structure of a best-of-three rather than on who won it. The motivation for looking inside a match rather than at its result is documented on both sides: play is not independent of the running score ( Klaassen & Magnus, (2001) ; Lago-Peñas & Gómez-López, (2014) ) , and the match stops as soon as one side reaches the target. Section 4.2 applies that logic to the half of a Counter-Strike map. 2.2 Measurement of Ability Revelation and the Remaining Gap The statistic is not ours. The measurement literature contains it under several names, and we adopt it in the form that literature established. Classical test theory defines reliability as the share of observed-score variance attributable to stable true-score differences ( Lord & Novick, (1968) ) . Signal-detection theory standardises the separation between two outcome distributions by their within-distribution noise ( Stanislaw & Todorov, (1999) ; Massof, (1987) ; DeCarlo, (2023) ) . In regression, signal variance relative to residual variance is Cohen’s f 2 f^{2} ( Cohen, (1988) ) . For the outcome M = α + β ​ S + ε M=\alpha+\beta S+\varepsilon , our D = β / σ ε D=\beta/\sigma_{\varepsilon} is the performance response to a one-unit rise in ability measured in residual standard deviations. When S S is standardised in a bivariate model D 2 D^{2} equals R 2 / ( 1 − R 2 ) R^{2}/(1-R^{2}) , reliability is D 2 / ( 1 + D 2 ) D^{2}/(1+D^{2}) , and for a contrast between two fixed ability levels β ​ Δ ​ S / σ ε \beta\Delta S/\sigma_{\varepsilon} is the discriminability d ′ d^{\prime} . The first of these identities is the signal-to-noise ratio of classical test theory, ρ / ( 1 − ρ ) \rho/(1-\rho) , whose equivalence with the information function of item response theory is established by Nicewander ((1993)) ; D D with a standardised S S is therefore also Cohen’s f f , and D D as we report it is f f expressed per 100 rating points rather than per standard deviation of ability. We keep D rather than R-squared because the latter also moves with the cross-sectional dispersion of ability, which differs across our two regimes. The statistic itself is standard; its application to a contest-format transition is not. The identity that matters most for the validity of what follows is with item response theory. Under a two-parameter normal-ogive model written in its latent-response form, the discrimination parameter of an item is exactly the slope of the latent-ability response divided by the residual standard deviation, a = λ / 1 − λ 2 a=\lambda/\sqrt{1-\lambda^{2}} for a standardised latent variable, and the information the item contributes to the ability estimate is proportional to its square ( Ferguson, (1949) ; Jordan & Spiess, (2019) ; Pavlech & Martinková, (2025) ) . Ferrando ((2012)) develops the same family of discrimination indices for the linear factor-analytic model, which is the case we are in: our outcome is continuous and our specification is linear, so the ratio β / σ ε \beta/\sigma_{\varepsilon} is the discrimination index of that model rather than an approximation to a binary-response one. Read a contest as an item that measures the latent ability of the competitors and D is that discrimination parameter, while the effective trial count of Section 4.2 is the information the contest carries. The correspondence is not an analogy constructed for this paper. Scale-invariance in the outcome, sensitivity to the units of the latent variable, and accumulation with the number of conditionally independent trials are properties established in that literature; we inherit them rather than assert them, and the interpretation of a cross-regime ratio of discriminations follows from them directly. The same ratio is what the tournament-design literature varies when it evaluates formats: the predictive power of Ryvkin & Ortmann ((2008)) is a monotone transformation of the gap in ability divided by the standard deviation of performance noise, so a format that raises D D is a format that more often selects the better competitor. The correction we apply for serial dependence is equally standard. The ratio of the observed variance of a half score to its binomial counterpart is the design effect of survey sampling, and the nominal number of rounds divided by it is the effective sample size ( Kish, (1965) ) . The same quantity appears in sports economics as the square of the Noll-Scully ratio of the actual to the idealised standard deviation of win percentages, whose dependence on the number of games played is well documented ( Owen, (2010) ) . Doria & Nalebuff ((2021)) make that dependence the object of study and construct measures of competitive balance that are invariant to season length, on the grounds that a measure moving mechanically with the amount of play cannot be compared across leagues that play different amounts. Our problem is the within-league form of theirs: because the treatment here is a change in the amount of play, a statistic that responds mechanically to length must be given a length-only benchmark before any residual movement can be read as substantive. Section 5.2 constructs that benchmark from the data rather than assuming independence, which is what the simulation literature on scoring systems typically assumes. Two clarifications keep the statistic where it belongs. First, discrimination in our sense is not the discriminatory power of contest theory. The parameter r of a Tullock contest success function, and the noise parameters that generalise it, govern how sensitively a modelled win probability responds to effort and are properties of an assumed functional form ( Amegashie, (2006) ; Jia, (2008) ) ; D is an estimated property of realised outcomes, and nothing in our design identifies r. Second, the empirical literature has measured objects of the same family without using this name. Lopez et al. ((2018)) and Wolfson et al. ((2018)) separate team strength from game-level noise; Heuer ((2020)) scores performance indicators by how much of the underlying team strength they recover net of statistical noise; Aoki et al. ((2017)) and Jerdee & Newman ((2024)) decompose outcomes into skill and luck, the latter with an explicit depth-of-competition parameter; Ben-Naim et al. ((2013)) work directly with the upset probability. Miles ((1984)) and its generalisation by Pollard ((2015)) evaluate scoring systems by the amount of play required to reach a given probability of identifying the better competitor, which is the same trade-off expressed as a cost rather than as a slope. We use D because it is estimable regime by regime from contests that were actually played and because its comparative static in length is sharp; we do not claim it improves on any of these. Evidence from implemented length changes remains scarce. Di Mattia & Krumer ((2026)) exploit a 2017 reform that cut round-robin matches per team in beach volleyball from three to two, and find no detectable change in favourite-win probability or in the alignment of final standings with initial strength. Theirs is the closest observed structural-change precedent, but the treatment varies the number of matches in a tournament stage rather than the number of repeated trials inside a single contest, and the outcome remains a win indicator. Esports research on tournament design largely imports methods built for traditional sport, and work on Counter-Strike concentrates on prediction, player valuation and in-game decisions. We found no scholarly analysis of the MR15-to-MR12 transition. The gap this paper fills is therefore not the proposition that shorter contests favour weaker competitors, which is well established. It is the measurement of ability revelation around an implemented transition, the separation of the ability-response and residual-noise components, and the comparison of the observed change with a mechanical benchmark calibrated on the effective number of rounds. Every element of the measurement apparatus is borrowed. What is new is that it is applied to a change in contest length that actually occurred, and that it is given a benchmark against which the estimate can fail. 3 Data 3.1 Source and Sample Construction The panel is assembled from HLTV.org, the reference results archive for professional Counter-Strike. It covers 1 January 2022 to 31 December 2025. The pipeline requests only URL families permitted by the site’s robots.txt: the paginated results archive, individual match pages, the weekly world-ranking archive and event pages. The date-filtered results view is disallowed, so the study window is located by binary search over the offset parameter of the unfiltered results list and then traversed page by page. Every page is stored in a compressed raw cache and every request is logged, so all downstream results can be re-derived without re-contacting the source. The crawl retrieved 34,453 match pages with no failures and no skipped observations. The window opens on 1 January 2022 rather than earlier for a substantive reason. Competitive play through 2020 and much of 2021 ran under pandemic restrictions: matches were played online, international travel was suspended for long stretches, and the circuit was segmented into regional brackets. Venue is a first-order determinant of play in this discipline — 18.1 per cent of our maps are at a LAN event and the indicator enters every map-level specification — and regional segmentation breaks the network of common opponents on which any rating recursion depends. 2022 is the first full year after the circuit returned to its normal calendar. The cost of that choice is that the rating recursion begins with the sample rather than before it, so ratings are least informative in the opening months of the panel. The raw panel contains 72,576 played maps and 17,820 unplayed slots across 34,453 matches, 2,547 teams and 2,451 events. Teams are identified by persistent site identifiers rather than names, so renamings and sponsor changes do not fragment a team’s history. Three exclusions define the estimation sample. We drop 1,446 walkover placeholders: a forfeit is recorded as a nominal 1-0 result on a map named “Default” with no round detail, and such records are not contests. Assigning the format by calendar date relative to the engine release on 27 September 2023 would introduce substantial measurement error. Several leagues finished their previous-generation seasons after that date, and some final scores are observationally identical across regimes: a map ending 16-14 is either an MR15 regulation result or an MR12 map decided in the first overtime. The format is instead inferred from the scoreline of the map itself. The source reports the half-by-half score of every map in the form (10:5; 6:8), and a half is always played to completion, so the rounds contested in the first half identify the regime directly. Where the half string is missing we infer the format from unambiguous final scores, then from the observed format of other maps in the same event, and only as a last resort from the calendar; each observation records which rule applied. In the estimation window 97.96 per cent of maps are classified from the half structure, 1.92 per cent from the event majority, 0.04 per cent from the final score and 0.08 per cent from the calendar. A consistency filter discards half evidence that cannot generate the map’s own final score; five maps are affected. The favourite is the team with the better official world ranking in force before the match. We collected the weekly ranking archive in full for 29 November 2021 to 29 December 2025: 214 consecutive snapshots and 53,211 team-week observations, with roughly 235 to 265 ranked teams per snapshot. Snapshots are located by following each page’s own previous-week link rather than by generating Mondays, which picks up two irregular publication gaps a calendar-based iterator would miss. Matches are linked to rankings by an as-of join with a strict no-look-ahead rule: the applicable snapshot is the latest published on a strictly earlier calendar day, and each team is looked up in that snapshot only, so a team absent from it counts as unranked rather than carrying forward a stale rank. The realised lag runs from one to eight days, median four. Both teams are ranked for 81.9 per cent of maps. One institutional caveat is in order. The HLTV ranking is the consensus reference in the discipline, but it is not the ranking Valve uses: Major invitations and seeding run off the Valve Regional Standings. We use the HLTV ranking because it is published weekly, archived back to 2012 and covers far more teams than the invitation lists, and because it defines the favourite rather than allocating anything. We define the discrimination of the contest as D = β σ ε . D\;=\;\frac{\beta}{\sigma_{\varepsilon}}. (2) The two ingredients have plain readings. The slope β \beta is the signal : how far the expected outcome moves when one competitor is better than the other. The residual standard deviation σ ε \sigma_{\varepsilon} is the noise : how far realised outcomes scatter around that expectation when the ability gap is held fixed. In the estimates below the signal is 3.16 rounds per hundred rating points and the noise 5.42 rounds, so the contest is noisy: a single map is a weak signal of which team is better, which is why the question of how many rounds to play has force at all. The intercept α \alpha is a level term and plays no part in D D ; Section 4.2 explains why it is not zero. D answers the question a contest designer faces: by how many noise standard deviations does the expected outcome move when the ability gap widens by one unit. Two properties of D are relevant for what follows. D is invariant to the scale of the performance outcome, so first-half margins measured over fifteen and twelve rounds can be compared directly. It is not invariant to the units of ability, so the comparison requires S to stay on a common pre-match rating scale across regimes — which is why the rating recursion in Section 4.3 updates on round shares rather than map results. Unlike an R-squared or a correlation, D does not rise merely because the sample happens to contain a more dispersed set of ability gaps. That distinction is not hypothetical in this application: Section 5.5 shows the dispersion of the ability gap rising by a quarter across the transition, which is enough to reverse the sign of every standardised measure. What makes D D testable rather than merely descriptive is that it has a sharp comparative static in contest length.
